did_you_know.text: In the Bible, the word “kohen” usually refers to a religious leader or worship official. Here it describes Jethro’s position in Midian.
The name Gershom is connected with the words “ger” (“stranger”) and “sham” (“there”), expressing Moses’ feeling of being a foreigner in a land that was not his homeland.
The name Eliezer combines the words “my God” and “help.” Names like this often preserve an important memory or express a family’s faith.
The phrase “mountain of God” serves here as an important landmark in the wilderness. Later in Exodus, this mountain is associated with the place where Israel receives the Torah.
The phrase “they asked one another about their well-being” describes more than a quick greeting; it suggests mutual concern after a separation or journey.

In the ancient world, a shared meal after a sacrifice could express closeness, gratitude, and peace among the participants. This meal therefore brings Jethro, Moses, Aaron, and Israel’s elders together.
The repeated expression “you will surely wear yourself out” intensifies the warning: if Moses carries everything alone, he may become exhausted and lose his strength.

The list of qualities shows that talent alone is not enough; leaders also need integrity, reverence for God, and freedom from greed. The groups of thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens create several levels of responsibility.

The system proposed to Moses resembles a division of authority: most matters are handled close to the people, while only difficult cases reach the main leader. This saves time and reduces pressure without removing the possibility of appeal.
